examples.problem_statement: Given 3x + 6y = 27 and x + 2y + z = 11, compare Quantity A: z + 5 with Quantity B: x + 2y - 2. (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.description: Rather than solving for three variables from two equations, divide the first equation through by 3 to expose the compound quantity x + 2y.

solution.result: The second equation is regrouped around the block x + 2y
solution.description: Rewrite the second equation so that x + 2y appears as a single block, which is what the first equation has just evaluated.
Substitute the value 9 for the block x + 2y inside the regrouped second equation.
Isolate z by subtracting 9 from both sides, giving the single unknown the comparison needs.
Evaluate Quantity A by putting the value of z just found into z + 5.
Evaluate Quantity B by reusing x + 2y = 9 from step 1 in place of the block x + 2y.
Compare the two numeric values obtained and see that neither quantity exceeds the other.

key_reminders: Dividing an entire equation by a common factor is legal and often reveals a reusable compound block such as x + 2y.
Three variables with two equations is still solvable when the extra variables only ever appear as one fixed block.
A quantitative comparison only needs each quantity's value, not the individual values of x and y.
common_mistakes: Declaring the answer (D) because there are three variables and only two equations, without first dividing 3x + 6y = 27 by 3.
Trying to solve separately for x and y, which is impossible and unnecessary here.

solution.result: The exponent is a multiple of 4
solution.description: Test the exponent for divisibility by 4: 51! already carries the factors 2 and 4, so any power of it is divisible by 4.

solution.result: 7 raised to any multiple of 4 ends in 1
solution.description: Apply the known unit-digit rule for powers of 7, whose cycle closes every 4 steps at 1.
Match this power to the 7^{4k} form established in step 2, since step 1 showed its exponent is a multiple of 4.

key_reminders: The unit digit of powers of 7 repeats with period 4, ending in 1 at every exponent that is a multiple of 4.
Only the exponent's remainder on division by 4 matters, never its actual size.
A factorial of 4 or more is automatically divisible by 4, and so is any power of it.
common_mistakes: Attempting to evaluate or estimate the astronomically large exponent 51!^{31!} instead of testing it modulo 4.
Using remainder 0 as if it meant the first term of the cycle (7) rather than the fourth term (1).

concept.technique_name: laws of indices with prime factorisation

examples.problem_statement: Find the value of \frac{2^{n} \times 6^{m+1} \times 10^{m-n} \times 15^{m+n-2}}{4^{m} \times 3^{2m+n} \times 25^{m-1}}. Options: 1) 2  2) 2/3  3) 1/3  4) 3  5) None of these

solution.description: Break every composite base in the numerator into its prime factors so the whole expression is written over the primes 2, 3 and 5 only.
Do the same prime-factor rewrite for the composite bases in the denominator, leaving 3^{2m+n} unchanged since it is already prime-based.
Collect the numerator's like bases by adding their exponents, which is what the product rule for indices permits.
Divide base by base, subtracting each denominator exponent from the matching numerator exponent.
Simplify the surviving exponents: the 5s cancel entirely, one factor of 2 remains on top and one factor of 3 remains below.

key_reminders: Reduce every base to primes before combining; only like bases may have their exponents added or subtracted.
a^{m} \times a^{n} = a^{m+n} and a^{m} \div a^{n} = a^{m-n}.
A base whose net exponent is 0 cancels out of the expression entirely.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that 6 and 10 and 15 each split into two different primes, so their exponents must be distributed to both.
Mis-signing the exponent of 3, where (2m+n-1) - (2m+n) = -1 gives a denominator factor, not a numerator one.

concept.technique_name: sum of an evenly spaced set via its middle term

examples.problem_statement: If x = 3, what is the sum of 2x, (2x + 1), (2x + 2), (2x + 3), and (2x + 4)?

solution.result: An evenly spaced sequence with common difference 1
solution.description: Instead of substituting x into all five terms, notice each term is exactly one more than the one before it.
Identify the middle term of the five, which for an evenly spaced set is also the set's average.
Plug x = 3 into that middle term alone to get the numeric average.
Multiply the average by the number of terms, since sum equals average times count.

key_reminders: In an evenly spaced set the average equals the middle term.
With an odd count of terms there is a single true middle term to read off.
common_mistakes: Substituting x = 3 into all five terms and adding, which works but wastes time and invites an arithmetic slip.
Taking 2x + 2 as the answer itself rather than as the average that still has to be multiplied by 5.

examples.problem_statement: During a single week, from Monday through Friday, tours will be conducted of a company's three divisions - Operations, Production, Sales. Exactly five tours will be conducted that week, one each day. The schedule must conform to these restrictions: each division is toured at least once; Operations is not toured on Monday; Production is not toured on Wednesday; Sales is toured on two consecutive days and on no other days; if Operations is toured on Thursday, then Production is toured on Friday. If in the week's tour schedule the division that is toured on Tuesday is also toured on Friday, then for which one of the following days must a tour of the Production division be scheduled? (A) Monday (B) Tuesday (C) Wednesday (D) Thursday (E) Friday

solution.result: One division occupies both Tuesday and Friday
solution.description: Take on the question's extra condition and ask which of the three divisions could occupy both Tuesday and Friday.
Rule out Sales, since Sales must be toured on two consecutive days only, and Tuesday and Friday are not consecutive.

solution.operation: P \text{ on Tue and Fri} \Rightarrow \text{two P and two S fill Tue-Fri} \Rightarrow O \text{ on Mon}
solution.result: Illegal, so P is ruled out
solution.description: Rule out Production too: two Ps plus the two consecutive Sales days would fill Tuesday through Friday, forcing Operations onto Monday, which the rules forbid.

solution.operation: \text{Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri} = P\; O\; S\; S\; O
solution.description: With Sales and Production eliminated, Operations takes Tuesday and Friday, and the book states the resulting arrangement is P O S S O - putting Production on Monday.

key_reminders: Sales occupies exactly two consecutive days, so it can never be the division repeated on two non-adjacent days.
Operations is never toured on Monday, which is the constraint that kills the Production-on-Tuesday-and-Friday branch.
Every division must appear at least once across the five days.
common_mistakes: Assuming the repeated Tuesday/Friday division could be Sales, forgetting that Sales' two days must be consecutive.
Missing that placing Production on both Tuesday and Friday leaves only Monday for Operations, which is barred.
